body.text: An MES (manufacturing execution system) is software designed for the factory. It coordinates, records and monitors production from raw materials to finished goods, and sits between the ERP and the plant control systems.
A disclosure before we continue: Cyrrus doesn't resell licenses or take commissions from any vendor. That's why we can compare without preferences.
What does an MES do?

It receives work orders from the ERP and schedules them by priorities and available resources; dispatches the work to lines and people; allocates and tracks labor, materials and machines; keeps a two-way data exchange with the floor to correct in real time; controls documents, quality and traceability by lot, serial or order number; and collects production data to measure performance. When finished, it returns the results to the ERP.
What is the difference between an MES and an ERP?

The ERP manages the business as a whole: long-term planning, purchasing, costing and customer orders. The MES manages execution on the plant floor. The ISA-95 standard (IEC 62264) describes how they communicate: it places the ERP at level 4 (business planning) and the MES at level 3 (manufacturing operations management), and focuses on the interface between the two.

body.text: When does a plant need an MES?

Not every plant does. These are the signals we look for: lot or serial traceability is a customer or regulatory requirement; quality is critical and defects are found late; the ERP's plan and what happens on the floor diverge and nobody sees it until month-end; downtime and cycle times are logged by hand; or several plants run on different rules. If none apply, a good production setup in the ERP may be enough.
What should leadership ask before investing?

Four things. First, which decision you can't make today for lack of plant data, and what not making it costs. Second, how it will integrate with the ERP, who maintains the interface and what happens when either changes. Third, the multi-year total cost, using the logic of what it costs to implement an enterprise system, including devices, plant networks and supervisors' time. And fourth, how go-live will happen without stopping production.

Start from your real process: type of production, number of plants, quality and traceability requirements, and the plant team available. Ask for demos with your own flows, visit similar customers' plants and weigh integration with your current ERP. Test the screen with real operators: if it gets in their way they won't use it, and an MES that isn't logged on time doesn't do its job.

body.text: A new system, a reorganization or a redesigned process reaches a group that does not use it as expected. In meetings it is called “resistance.” This guide offers another reading: resistance is information about where the change got stuck, and it can be diagnosed.

A note on what follows: the model and the sponsor behaviors come from Prosci and Kotter, cited at the end. The diagnostic questions and suggested actions are Cyrrus's judgment, not the results of a study.
What is resistance to change?

It is people's reaction when a change asks them to give up a familiar way of working. It can look like slow compliance, doubts that go unspoken, or open rejection. Treating it as a character flaw can lead to persuading or pressuring; treating it as a signal makes it possible to ask what that group lacks in order to move forward.
How do you diagnose it with ADKAR?

Prosci's ADKAR describes five things each person needs to change: awareness (understanding why the change is needed), desire (choosing to participate in and support it), knowledge (knowing how to change and what success requires), ability (putting new skills and behaviors into practice) and reinforcement (sustaining the new way and preventing backsliding). Prosci proposes identifying the earliest barrier and focusing support where people need it most.
Where the change gets stuck and what to ask (Cyrrus's judgment)
rows: Can you explain in your own words why this is changing?
Leadership explains the why and listens to doubts
What do you gain and lose with the change?
Group conversations, addressing what is lost and showing what is gained
Do you know what to do differently from Monday?
Role-based training with real situations from their work
Can you do it in your daily work, with the time and tools you have?
Supported practice and a network of support users
What happens if you go back to the old way?
Real-usage indicators, recognition and follow-up after go-live

body.text: Order matters: training a group that does not yet understand why it is changing, or does not want to, does not resolve the stall. That is why you look first for the earliest element that is not covered.
What falls to leadership?

Prosci has identified active and visible sponsorship as the top contributor to change success for over 25 years, and in its most recent study places it there by a three-to-one margin. Among the practices it recommends for the sponsor are direct communication with employees (face-to-face conversations, speeches or videos), agreeing on activities by phase and audience, and holding the sponsor accountable with clear objectives. Kotter, for his part, starts by creating a sense of urgency, and his fifth step asks to enable action by removing obstacles that slow things down or create roadblocks.
What should you do when resistance is already there?

Four practical steps, based on Cyrrus's judgment. First, listen group by group before acting, with questions like those in the table. Second, find the earliest element that is not covered and address it before the others. Third, remove the obstacles the company itself created: no time to learn, incomplete tools or managers who do not use the new way. Fourth, show small, real progress: Kotter calls it generating short-term wins.
Mistakes to avoid
Answering everything with more training without knowing whether people lack understanding, willingness or ability.
Leaving the conversation to HR or IT, with leadership not speaking to the teams.
Declaring the change finished at go-live, with no reinforcement period.

body.text: Someone copies data from an email into a spreadsheet and then types it into the ERP. It is repetitive and rule-based. RPA exists for that kind of task. This guide explains what it is, how it differs from artificial intelligence and what leadership should check before investing.

A note: the definitions and limits come from IBM and Microsoft Learn, cited at the end. The questions and recommendations for deciding are Cyrrus's judgment, not study results. We include no savings figures because we have no primary source to back them.
What is RPA?

RPA is robotic process automation. IBM describes it as using automation technologies to take over repetitive office tasks that people normally do. Microsoft, in the Power Automate documentation, presents it as a way to automate repetitive tasks on a computer, including legacy applications, using interface elements, images or coordinates.

According to IBM, bots work on the presentation layer of existing applications, so they can be used where no API exists. That is its practical advantage: it does not force you to change the system you already have.
How is it different from artificial intelligence?

IBM sums it up: RPA is process-driven, whereas AI is data-driven. RPA bots only follow the processes a user defined; AI uses machine learning to find patterns, especially in unstructured data, and improves over time.
RPA versus AI (per IBM; the last row is Cyrrus's judgment)
rows: Repetitive task, clear rules, stable inputs
Messy data or decisions that do not fit a rule

body.text: In practice they can be combined: AI interprets a document and RPA loads the result into the system. But they are two separate investment decisions.
When does RPA make sense?

When the task is repetitive, follows rules that can be written down and runs on systems that will not change soon. IBM mentions uses such as claims processing in insurance, account opening in banking or order management in retail. Microsoft cites data entry into an ERP as an example.
When does it not?

IBM points to limits: RPA only follows defined processes and can be hard to scale in an enterprise when regulations or internal operations change. Based on that, Cyrrus recommends asking before you buy:
Does the process change often? If it changes every quarter, the bot will need constant adjustment.
Is the problem the process or the task? If the process has unnecessary steps, redesign it before automating it.
Is there a direct way to connect the systems? If the ERP and CRM can be integrated, an integration may be steadier than a bot copying data through the screen.
What should leadership decide?

Four decisions, per Cyrrus's judgment. First, which process and why: choose by business impact. Second, who is responsible for the bot when the process changes. Third, what is measured to know it works (time, errors, exceptions). Fourth, who oversees what the bot does, especially if it touches financial or customer data.

body.text: A company grows and its customer data ends up scattered across spreadsheets, emails and each salesperson's memory. That is when a CRM gets bought. This guide explains what it is, which types exist, which risks the sources acknowledge and what leadership should check before choosing.

A note: the definitions, types and risks come from IBM and Microsoft's documentation, cited at the end. The selection criteria are Cyrrus's judgment, not study results. We include no return figures because we have no primary source to back them.
What is a CRM?

CRM stands for customer relationship management. IBM defines it as a set of integrated technologies used to document, track and manage an organization's relationships with existing and potential customers. In the Dynamics 365 Sales documentation, Microsoft describes it as the tool to keep track of accounts and contacts, move a sale from lead to order, create marketing lists and campaigns and follow service cases.
Which types of CRM exist?
IBM distinguishes three types, which are not mutually exclusive:
Types of CRM according to IBM
rows: Customer interactions: sales, service and marketing automation
The most common; its success depends on the organization's data entry

Better suited to mid-sized and large organizations; may require skilled staff

body.text: IBM also notes that a CRM can be installed on the company's own infrastructure, used in the cloud or customized.
What problems does it solve?

According to IBM, a CRM lets you track leads and the sales pipeline on a single dashboard, forecast sales, manage communication with prospects and analyze the frequency, volume and outcome of follow-ups. IBM also credits it with benefits such as better customer segmentation, higher retention and less time spent searching for information. These are benefits described by the source; each company's result depends on how it uses the system.
What risks do the sources acknowledge?

IBM points to three. First, adoption: staff must be trained or may resist the new system, and sales leadership is key to getting it used. Second, the vendor: switching vendors can significantly increase costs. Third, size: cost and benefit estimates are less accurate for larger projects.
How do you choose the right CRM?

Five criteria, per Cyrrus's judgment. First, the process: describe how you sell today and what you want to change before looking at products. Second, the users: choose with the daily user in mind, not the buyer. Third, integration: define which data must be shared with the ERP and invoicing. Fourth, total cost over several years: licenses, implementation, integrations and training. Fifth, the exit: ask how data is exported if you ever change vendors.

Third, how it connects to the ERP so that customer, order and invoice are not entered twice. Fourth, how you will measure that the team is actually using it.

body.text: A salesperson closes an order in the CRM and someone types it again into the ERP. Billing invoices one price and sales quoted another. This guide explains what a connector shipped by the vendor can do, using the example documented by Microsoft, and what leadership must decide before connecting the two systems.

A note: the only case with an open source that we reviewed for this guide is Business Central with Dynamics 365 Sales, in Microsoft Learn (cited at the end). That page does not use the word middleware or compare other ways to integrate. For other combinations, such as an SAP ERP with a Salesforce or HubSpot CRM, we claim nothing: ask the vendor for its documentation. The decision criteria are Cyrrus's judgment.
What is a native connector?

It is an integration that the system's vendor ships and documents, rather than third-party integration software. In Microsoft's case, the documentation states that Business Central integrates with Dynamics 365 Sales through Dataverse, and that a first-time integration must be done that way. The connection is set up with an assisted setup guide inside Business Central.
Which data does it sync?
Microsoft's documentation lists a standard mapping between tables in the two systems:
Standard mapping between Business Central and Dynamics 365 Sales, per Microsoft
rows: Both ways, if bidirectional sync is turned on

body.text: Microsoft also describes a scheduled job that updates item availability every 30 minutes and synchronization jobs with a default frequency of 30 minutes. In other words, information is not updated instantly: there is a frequency you must accept or adjust.
Which limits and conditions does the source state?
Among the conditions listed in the documentation:
There are two ways to synchronize sales orders, the legacy one (only from Sales to Business Central) and the bidirectional one, and they cannot be used at the same time.
Changes made by the integration user account are not synchronized, so Microsoft recommends not changing data with that account.
If you reconnect through Dataverse, the default synchronization settings are applied and existing configurations are overwritten.
To sync items with different units of measure you must turn on a separate option, and Microsoft notes that Dynamics 365 Sales does not allow changing a product's unit group.
What should leadership decide, whatever the connector?

Five decisions, per Cyrrus's judgment. First, which system is the master for each piece of data: customer, price, inventory and invoice often have different owners. Second, in which direction each piece flows. Third, which update frequency the business needs: what the salesperson sees must be current when quoting. Fourth, who answers when synchronization fails. Fifth, what happens with duplicate or incomplete data before connecting: a connector does not fix it.
For the last point, see the guide on data governance and deduplication in the CRM.

body.text: When is it worth looking at another option?

When the vendor's connector does not cover your company's processes, when the systems come from different vendors with no documented integration, or when the business needs rules the connector does not allow. In those cases the alternative is a custom integration or integration software, with its own cost and upkeep. Ask each vendor for its documentation and its list of data and limits, and add them to the project's total cost.

Which costs do those figures leave out?
The pages themselves say so:

Salesforce: the pricing page publishes no implementation price; it mentions professional services and certified partners. Six items, per Cyrrus's judgment: licenses (users times price times 12 months times the years analyzed), add-ons and credits, onboarding or implementation, integrations (with the ERP and other tools), training and change management, and the internal team that administers the system. The last four have no published price: they are obtained by getting quotes and estimating the team's time.

body.text: The same customer appears three times in the CRM: with the full name, with an acronym and with another person's email. Each salesperson sees part of the history. This guide explains how two widely used platforms detect duplicates, per their own documentation, and what leadership should define.

A note: the features, limits and requirements come from Microsoft Learn and the HubSpot knowledge base, cited at the end. We did not review Salesforce's documentation because its help page could not be opened. The governance recommendations are Cyrrus's judgment.
How does Dynamics 365 detect duplicates?

According to Microsoft, the Dynamics 365 Sales and Customer Service apps include default duplicate detection rules for accounts and contacts, but not for other record types. To detect duplicates in other records you must create new rules and turn them on.

A rule lets you choose the record type, the fields and the comparison criterion, for example exact match, same first characters or same last characters, whether it is case-sensitive, whether it ignores blank fields and whether it excludes inactive records. Microsoft recommends basing the criterion on a field with unique values, such as email. Five rules can be published at a time for the same base record type.
How does HubSpot do it?

HubSpot states that it compares property values daily to surface possible duplicates. By default, contacts are compared on fields such as name, email, phone, zip code and company, and companies on domain, name, country, phone and industry. Pairs can be reviewed one by one or in bulk and merged or rejected. A HubSpot warning: merged records cannot be reverted.
According to the same page, custom rules, the audit log and bulk management at larger volumes require its Data Hub product, which is another subscription.

Second, the matching criterion: which fields make two records the same customer (email, domain, tax ID). Third, who approves a merge and which record prevails, knowing that in HubSpot it cannot be undone. Fourth, which fields are mandatory when creating a record and from which sources data comes in. Fifth, a periodic review routine with an indicator that someone watches.

body.text: Who is accountable if an AI tool your team uses makes a bad decision? Governing AI means defining who decides, by what criteria and with what evidence. This guide summarizes three public references for doing it and what leadership has to decide.

A note: what we say about each framework comes from the official pages of NIST, the OECD and the IEC (cited at the end, consulted in November 2026). We could not open the standard’s page on iso.org (it returned a 403 error), so for ISO/IEC 42001 we state only what the IEC publishes; the text of the standard is paid and we did not review it. The recommendations on what to decide are Cyrrus’s judgment.
What is AI governance?

In the sources we reviewed we found no single definition, and we do not invent one. What the three frameworks share is putting management rules around the use of AI: NIST speaks of managing risks to individuals, organizations and society; the OECD, of promoting innovative and trustworthy AI; ISO/IEC 42001, of a management system inside the organization. In this article “AI governance” is used in that broad sense (Cyrrus’s judgment).
NIST AI RMF: a voluntary risk framework

NIST (the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology) released version 1.0 of its AI Risk Management Framework on January 26, 2023 (document NIST.AI.100-1). Its official page says the framework is intended for voluntary use, and the document itself describes it as voluntary, rights-preserving, non-sector-specific and use-case agnostic. The page also notes that version 1.0 is being revised as part of the White House AI Action Plan, so check which version is current.

The framework’s core has four functions, per NIST: govern, map, measure and manage. Govern is a cross-cutting function infused throughout AI risk management; map establishes the context to frame the risks of a system; measure uses tools and methods to analyze, assess, benchmark and monitor AI risk; manage allocates resources to the risks already mapped and measured.

The document lists the characteristics of trustworthy AI: valid and reliable; safe; secure and resilient; accountable and transparent; explainable and interpretable; privacy-enhanced; and fair, with harmful bias managed. NIST also published a Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1, July 26, 2024) and a companion Playbook.
OECD principles: shared values for trustworthy AI

According to the OECD page, the principles were adopted in May 2019 and updated in May 2024. The OECD describes them as the first intergovernmental standard on AI. They are five values-based principles: inclusive growth, sustainable development and well-being; human rights and democratic values, including fairness and privacy; transparency and explainability; robustness, security and safety; and accountability.

The OECD also lists five recommendations for policymakers: investing in AI research and development, fostering an inclusive AI-enabling ecosystem, shaping an interoperable governance and policy environment, building human capacity and preparing for labour-market transition, and international co-operation. For a company, the practical use of the principles is Cyrrus’s judgment: to set the values that an internal policy and a management system then turn into rules.
ISO/IEC 42001: a standard for managing AI as a system

The IEC publishes ISO/IEC 42001:2023, “Information technology — Artificial intelligence — Management system”, edition 1.0, dated December 18, 2023, 51 pages, from technical committee ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 42. According to its listing, it specifies requirements and gives guidance for establishing, implementing, maintaining and continually improving an AI management system within an organization, and it applies to any organization, regardless of size, type and nature, that provides or uses products or services that use AI systems.

To audit and certify against ISO/IEC 42001 there is a companion standard, ISO/IEC 42006, which according to Estonia’s standards body (citing the IEC) sets additional requirements for bodies that audit and certify AI management systems. We go into more detail in our guide to ISO/IEC 42001.
What leadership needs to decide

Four decisions, from Cyrrus’s judgment and not from the cited sources. First, which framework you will use as a reference and for what: managing risks (NIST), setting values (OECD) or certifying a management system (ISO/IEC 42001); they can be combined. body.text: Which rules apply to the AI your company uses? It depends on where you offer products or services and on whom the AI is used. This guide gathers what official sources say and is clear about what we could not verify.

A note: every fact comes from an official text or page cited at the end, consulted in November 2026. Rules change often (the EU regulation itself was amended in July 2026), so confirm the current version before deciding. This is not legal advice; what is Cyrrus’s judgment, we say so.
European Union: the AI Act

According to the European Commission, the AI Act entered into force on August 1, 2024 and defines four levels of risk: unacceptable risk (prohibited practices), high risk, transparency risk (for example, telling a person they are interacting with a chatbot) and minimal or no risk, for which no rules are introduced.

Application is staged. The Commission states that the AI Omnibus, an amendment to the regulation, entered into force on July 27, 2026 and extended the deadlines for high-risk systems. The table summarizes the dates published by the Commission and the consolidated text as of July 27, 2026.
Application dates of the AI Act, per the European Commission and the consolidated text
rows: Prohibited practices and AI literacy obligations
Governance and obligations for general-purpose AI models
Some new Article 5 prohibitions (added by the Omnibus)
High-risk systems under Annex I (regulated products)

body.text: Penalties under the EU regulation

Article 99, in the text published by the European Commission’s AI Act Service Desk, sets these maximums: for prohibited practices, up to EUR 35 million or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher; for other operator obligations, up to EUR 15 million or 3%; and for incorrect, incomplete or misleading information to authorities, up to EUR 7.5 million or 1%. For SMEs, including start-ups, the lower of the two figures applies.
United States: two state examples
We did not review U.S. federal rules for this guide. The two examples below were read from each state’s official text or page.

Texas: H.B. 149, short title Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act, states that it “takes effect January 1, 2026.” The attorney general has exclusive authority to enforce it, and the law says it gives no private right of action. Before suing, the attorney general must give notice and wait 60 days for the violation to be cured. Civil penalties are $10,000 to $12,000 per curable violation, $80,000 to $200,000 per uncurable violation and $2,000 to $40,000 for each day a violation continues.

Colorado: the official page for bill SB26-189, “Automated Decision-Making Technology,” shows it as a law signed on May 14, 2026. Per that summary, it repeals and reenacts provisions of SB 24-205 and regulates automated decision-making technology in consequential decisions about education, employment, housing, financial or lending services, insurance, health care and essential government services. Developers must give technical documentation to those who deploy the technology; deployers must notify people, explain an adverse outcome in plain language and recognize rights of access, correction and human review. The attorney general enforces it and it creates no new private right of action. The page states that developer documentation requirements start on January 1, 2027 and that the attorney general must adopt rules by that date.
Spain: a supervisory agency

Royal Decree 729/2023 of August 22, published in the BOE no. 210 of September 2, 2023, created the Spanish Agency for the Supervision of Artificial Intelligence (AESIA) as a public-law entity headquartered in A Coruña. Its Article 4.1 assigns it supervision, advisory, awareness-raising and training tasks. We did not review what powers the EU regulation gives it or any rules after 2023; for its current status, check with the agency itself.
Colombia: a national policy

Colombia’s DNP describes CONPES document 4144, the National Artificial Intelligence Policy, approved on February 14, 2025. Per that page, it aims to make Colombia a reference in the use, development and adoption of AI, with more than 100 actions through 2030 and an investment of $479,000 million (as written by the DNP); MinTIC, DAPRE, MinCiencias and the DNP lead its implementation. It is an explanatory article by the DNP, not the text of the CONPES. We did not review the full document, so we do not state whether it imposes obligations on companies.
What leadership should review

Three questions, from Cyrrus’s judgment. First, in which countries you offer products or services that use AI, or use AI on people, because that determines which rules apply. Second, whether any of your systems make or support decisions on employment, credit, health or insurance, which are examples that appear in Colorado’s law, and whether they could fall into a high-risk category under the EU regulation. Third, who in the company follows regulatory changes and how often.

body.text: When a client or partner asks whether your company “complies with ISO 42001,” it helps to know what that standard is before answering. This guide gathers what can be stated from open sources.

A note: the data on the standard comes from the IEC listing and from an article by Estonia’s standards body that cites the IEC (both at the end, consulted in November 2026). The standard’s page on iso.org returned a 403 error and the full text is paid, so we did not review it and do not describe its clauses. What is Cyrrus’s judgment, we say so.
What is ISO/IEC 42001?

According to the IEC listing, ISO/IEC 42001:2023 specifies requirements and gives guidance for establishing, implementing, maintaining and continually improving an AI management system within an organization. It is an international standard, not a law.
ISO/IEC 42001:2023 listing, per the IEC
rows: Information technology — Artificial intelligence — Management system

body.text: Who does it apply to?

The IEC listing says it applies to any organization, regardless of size, type and nature, that provides or uses products or services that utilize AI systems. In other words, it is not limited to those who develop AI: it includes those who use it.
Can you be certified?

Estonia’s standards body, citing the IEC, reports that ISO/IEC 42006 defines additional requirements for bodies that audit and certify AI management systems against ISO/IEC 42001, and that it builds on ISO/IEC 17021-1 without replacing it. In other words, a standard exists for those who certify. We did not review which certifiers are accredited in your country or what a certification costs or how long it takes: we have no primary source and give no figures.
What we do not state

We do not describe the requirements by clause or the standard’s controls, because we did not read the text. Nor do we state that meeting it equals meeting the EU AI Act or any other law: we found no official equivalence in the sources reviewed. If a vendor or adviser tells you otherwise, ask for the source.

The same goes for its relationship with the NIST framework: they are different documents, one a voluntary risk management framework and the other a management system standard, and any mapping between them would be our own judgment.
What leadership needs to decide

Four questions, from Cyrrus’s judgment. First, who is asking and what they expect: a certificate, or alignment with the standard. Second, which AI systems fall within scope, those you build and those you only use. Third, who will be the owner inside the company. Fourth, who will pay for the audit; any figure should come from a quote, not a rule of thumb.

body.text: How prepared is your company to govern AI? A maturity model sorts the answer into levels. This guide explains how a model published by Microsoft is built and how to use it well.

A note: the only model we describe is Microsoft’s Responsible AI Maturity Model (report MSR-TR-2023-26, version 1 of May 17, 2023), read on its Microsoft Research page and in its document (cited at the end, consulted in November 2026). It measures maturity in responsible AI, a topic close to governance but not identical. In our search, the other “AI governance maturity” models were from consultancies and vendors and we found no single official standard; we did not use them. What is Cyrrus’s judgment, we say so.
What is a maturity model?

Microsoft presents its model as a framework to help organizations identify their current and desired levels of responsible AI maturity, and describes it as a map of a complex, evolving territory, not as a measure. In general (Cyrrus’s judgment), a maturity model sorts practices into levels to decide where to go next.
How Microsoft’s model is built

It has 24 dimensions derived empirically from interviews and focus groups with more than 90 responsible AI specialists and AI practitioners. Each dimension has five levels, from 1 to 5: Latent, Emerging, Developing, Realizing and Leading. The dimensions are grouped into three categories.
Categories and some dimensions of the model, per its document
rows: Leadership and culture; governance; responsible AI policy; compliance processes and infrastructure; knowledge resources; tooling
Teams valuing responsible AI; timing of responsible AI in the lifecycle; motivation for AI products; cross-discipline collaboration
Accountability; external and internal transparency; identifying, measuring, mitigating and monitoring risks; AI privacy and security

body.text: Per the document, organizational foundations are the base of the other two categories, and the dimensions depend on each other: progress on one can depend on the maturity of others.
Usage rules the document itself gives

Microsoft recommends using the model as a map for guidance and not as a measurement tool for punitive purposes; not calculating an overall score or averaging across dimensions, because some weigh more than others (a level 5 in tooling does not have the same impact as a level 5 in culture and leadership); using it to supplement, not replace, other AI, security and privacy maturity models; and having both senior leaders and team members respond, treating differences in perception as a signal of room to improve.

It also warns that progress between levels is not linear: moving out of levels 1 and 2 can require creating new processes, which is resource-intensive, while moving out of levels 3 and 4 may just be formalizing or integrating what already exists. It adds that level 5 may not be applicable or desirable for every organization and that all criteria of one level should be met before moving to the next.
What it does not solve

The document is from May 2023, before the EU AI Act entered into force (August 1, 2024), and describes itself as a living artifact that will continue to evolve. We did not see in it a mapping to that regulation or to ISO/IEC 42001; any mapping would be our own judgment. We include no benchmark figures across companies because we have no primary source to back them.
What leadership needs to decide

Three decisions, from Cyrrus’s judgment. First, which dimensions to address first; the document places organizational foundations (leadership, governance, policy) as the base for the others. Second, who answers for each dimension. Third, how often to repeat the assessment and who reviews it. Use it as the starting point for a conversation, not as a grade.
To see the frameworks that accompany a maturity model and how to evaluate tools, read what AI governance is and which frameworks to use and how to evaluate governance tools.

body.text: What would an authority, a client or an auditor ask for if they asked how you govern the AI you use? This guide starts from what the EU AI Act documents and turns it into what evidence is worth having at hand.

A note: the articles cited are from the text consolidated as of July 27, 2026 published by the European Commission’s AI Act Service Desk, and what is said about AI literacy comes from the Commission’s questions and answers (both at the end, consulted in November 2026). The evidence column is Cyrrus’s judgment; it is not legal advice and does not say what applies to your company, which depends on its role and its systems.
First: are you a provider or a deployer?

Article 3 defines the provider as a natural or legal person, public authority or other body that develops an AI system, or has it developed, and places it on the market. The deployer is whoever uses an AI system under its authority, except in a personal non-professional activity. A company can be both depending on the system. The same article defines an AI system as a machine-based system designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy, that may exhibit adaptiveness after deployment and that infers, from the input it receives, how to generate outputs, such as predictions, that can influence physical or virtual environments.
Second: is any system high-risk?

Under Article 6, an AI system is high-risk when it is a safety component of an Annex I product, or is itself such a product, and the product must undergo third-party conformity assessment; or when it is listed in Annex III. An Annex III system is not considered high-risk if it poses no significant risk of harm, for example if it performs a narrow procedural task, but that exception does not apply if the system profiles natural persons.
Under Article 113 in its current version, the Annex III high-risk rules apply from December 2, 2027 and the Annex I rules from August 2, 2028. The full dates are in our guide to AI regulation.
What the regulation documents and what evidence to keep
AI Act obligations and suggested evidence (the evidence is Cyrrus’s judgment)
rows: Providers and deployers take measures to support the AI literacy of their staff and other persons operating or using AI systems on their behalf
For high-risk systems, a risk management system established, implemented, documented and maintained, as a continuous iterative process throughout the lifecycle
Risk register, decisions and dated reviews
Drawn up before the system is placed on the market or put into service, kept up to date and containing at least the elements of Annex IV
High-risk systems must be technically capable of automatically logging events over the lifetime of the system
Proof that logs are generated and where they are stored
High-risk systems are designed so that natural persons can effectively oversee them while in use
Designation of the people who oversee and their training

Providers of high-risk systems put in place a quality management system covering, among other aspects, a compliance strategy, data management, risk management, post-market monitoring and an accountability framework
Use the system per its instructions, assign human oversight to people with competence, training and authority, monitor its operation and keep the logs under their control for at least six months
List of systems, owners, reviews and retained logs

body.text: Article 26 adds that deployers must inform workers’ representatives and the affected workers before using a high-risk system in the workplace, inform people subject to decisions supported by Annex III systems, notify the provider or distributor and the market surveillance authority without undue delay if they see a risk and suspend use of the system, report serious incidents immediately and cooperate with the competent authorities.
AI literacy: what the Commission clarifies

According to the European Commission’s questions and answers, Article 4 applies from February 2, 2025 and contains no strict requirements or mandatory trainings: it does not require guaranteeing a specific level of AI literacy for any person, nor a certificate, and the organization can keep an internal record of trainings and other initiatives. The Commission adds that relying only on instructions for use may be ineffective. National market surveillance authorities could impose proportionate penalties, with supervision and enforcement from August 2, 2026, and the regulation creates no criminal offences or right to compensation.
Penalties and who decides

The regulation’s maximum fines are in Article 99 and we summarize them in the regulation guide. Which systems are high-risk, what role your company has and what applies to it are decisions that require legal analysis; this article does not make them for you.
What leadership needs to decide

Four decisions, from Cyrrus’s judgment. First, who builds and maintains the list of AI systems, with the company’s role in each. Second, who answers for the evidence in each row of the table. Third, how often it is reviewed and who approves it. Fourth, when to consult a legal adviser, before anyone outside asks for the evidence.
To choose what supports all this, read how to evaluate governance tools; to place yourself on a readiness scale, see the maturity model.

A note: we do not name or compare products, nor give prices, because we have no primary source to state what a specific vendor offers. First: what needs to be governed

Five questions, from Cyrrus’s judgment. Where the data is hosted and who accesses it. Which standards it claims to meet and with what evidence, not just a logo. Three decisions, from Cyrrus’s judgment. First, what specific problem the tool will solve: inventory, risks, documentation, logs or training. Second, who will own the tool and the evidence it stores. body.text: Monday, 9 a.m., and the ERP doesn't respond. No one knows whether last night's backup works, who authorizes working with spreadsheets in the meantime, or whom to call at the vendor. That scenario is the one a business continuity plan should have resolved before it happens.

This guide explains what a business continuity plan is, how it differs from a disaster recovery plan and a contingency plan, what the business impact analysis (BIA) is, what RTO and RPO mean, what ISO 22301 says and which decisions belong to leadership. The definitions come from two official sources: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 and ISO's page on the 22301 standard.
What is a business continuity plan?

A business continuity plan (BCP) is the plan that defines how an organization keeps operating when a disruption affects its critical processes. According to NIST SP 800-34, the BCP focuses on sustaining an organization's mission/business processes during and after a disruption; it may be written for the processes of a single business unit or address the entire organization's processes, and it may be scoped to only the functions deemed priorities.

The same guide clears up a frequent confusion: continuity planning normally applies to the business itself — the ability to continue critical functions and processes during and after an emergency — while contingency planning normally applies to information systems and provides the steps to recover their operation.
What is the difference between a continuity plan, a DRP and a contingency plan?
They are three different plans that must be coordinated. NIST SP 800-34 describes them this way:
Business continuity plan (BCP): sustains business processes during and after a disruption. It is leadership's plan.

Disaster recovery plan (DRP): applies to major, usually physical, disruptions that deny access to the primary facility for an extended period. It is an information-system-focused plan designed to restore operability of the target system, application or infrastructure at an alternate site after an emergency.

Information system contingency plan (ISCP): provides established procedures for the assessment and recovery of a specific system following a disruption, with roles, inventory, recovery procedures and testing. Unlike the DRP, it can be activated at the system's current location or at an alternate site.
The BCP belongs to the business; the DRP and contingency plans belong to IT. Without the first, the other two restore systems that perhaps no one needed first.
What is the business impact analysis (BIA)?

The business impact analysis is the step that turns continuity into something measurable. According to NIST SP 800-34, the BIA's purpose is to correlate the system with the critical mission/business processes and services it provides and, based on that information, characterize the consequences of a disruption.

The guide describes three steps. First, determine the business processes the system supports and their recovery criticality, along with the outage impacts and estimated downtime, which should reflect the maximum time the organization can tolerate. Second, identify the resources required to resume those processes: facilities, personnel, equipment, software, data files, system components and vital records. Third, identify recovery priorities for system resources, to establish the order in which each one is recovered.
In practice, the BIA is a conversation with process owners and leadership, not an IT exercise: they are the ones who know what each hour without invoicing, shipping or running payroll costs.
What are the RTO, the RPO and the MTD?
Three measures come out of the BIA, which NIST SP 800-34 defines as follows:

Maximum Tolerable Downtime (MTD): the total amount of time the system owner or authorizing official is willing to accept for a business process outage or disruption, including all impact considerations.

Recovery Time Objective (RTO): the maximum amount of time a system resource can remain unavailable before there is an unacceptable impact on other system resources, the business processes it supports and the MTD. Because the RTO must ensure the MTD is not exceeded, it must normally be shorter than the MTD.

Recovery Point Objective (RPO): the point in time, prior to a disruption or outage, to which business process data can be recovered given the most recent backup copy. Unlike the RTO, it is not considered part of the MTD: it is a factor of how much data loss the business process can tolerate.

The guide adds a useful idea for leadership: the shorter the RTO, the more expensive the recovery solutions. A system that must be recovered immediately requires redundancy and alternate sites; a low-impact system with a long RTO can be handled with a simple backup. The balance point between the cost of disruption and the cost to recover is different for every organization and every system.
What does ISO 22301 say?

ISO 22301:2019 is the international standard for business continuity management systems (BCMS). According to ISO's official page, it provides a framework for organizations to plan, establish, implement, operate, monitor, review, maintain and continually improve a documented management system to protect against, reduce the likelihood of, and ensure recovery from disruptive incidents. Its second edition was published in October 2019 and has a 2024 amendment.

Certification is not mandatory. It makes sense when a customer, a bank or the sector requires it. What is worthwhile, in our view, is building the plan with the logic of a management system — owners, documentation, tests and periodic review — even if the company never certifies.
How do you build a business continuity plan, step by step?
NIST SP 800-34 describes a seven-step process for information system contingency planning, which also works as a structure for the continuity plan:
1. Develop the policy: objectives, scope, roles and responsibilities, and the frequency of testing and maintenance.
2. Conduct the business impact analysis (BIA): critical processes, impacts, resources and recovery priorities.
3. Identify preventive controls: measures that reduce the effects of a disruption before it happens.
4. Create contingency strategies: backups, alternate sites, roles and cost considerations, integrated into the architecture.
5. Develop the plan: document the recovery strategy with detailed procedures.
6. Test, train and exercise: rehearse the plan, train personnel and run drills.
7. Maintain the plan: review and update it when systems, processes or the organization change.
A continuity plan that hasn't been tested isn't a plan. The drill shows in hours what the document doesn't show in months.
What must leadership decide?

There are decisions the IT department cannot make alone. Which processes are critical and in what order they are recovered. How long each one tolerates being down (MTD and RTO) and how much data it can lose (RPO). How much the company is willing to invest in redundancy versus the cost of the disruption. Who activates the plan, who communicates with customers and authorities, and who decides to return to normal. And how often it is rehearsed.

What does belong to IT is the DRP: which systems are restored, with which backups, at which site and with which procedures. The two parts must fit: the DRP recovers what the BIA said was critical, in the order and times leadership set.
How we can help

If the plan requires new backup, high-availability or alternate-site solutions, we select them with our technology infrastructure consulting, with no vendor commissions, and Project Management governs the implementation. body.text: The question arrives at the budget committee: sales wants a CRM, operations a maintenance system, finance wants to replace the ERP, and someone proposes 'doing something with AI'. Each proposal makes sense on its own. What doesn't exist is the criterion to decide which comes first, how they connect to each other and what each contributes to the business plan.
This guide explains what an IT strategy is, what it is for, what it should include, what two public IT governance frameworks say and how it is built step by step.
What is IT strategy?

An IT strategy is the plan that defines which technology a company needs to execute its business strategy, in what order it will adopt it and with what business case. It starts from the business — what the company wants to achieve, which processes sustain it — and ends in a portfolio of technology initiatives (ERP, CRM, data, artificial intelligence, infrastructure) with owners, sequence and multi-year costs.
It is not a systems inventory or each department's wish list. It is a leadership decision about where to invest in technology and where not to, with the same criteria used for any other investment.
What is an IT strategy for?

It serves three purposes. First, so that technology responds to a business objective and not to a vendor's catalog: each initiative is justified by what it changes in operations or revenue. Second, so that systems are decided together and not one at a time: a CRM that doesn't integrate with the ERP, or an AI project with no governed data, are the result of deciding project by project. Third, so that the board can approve a technology budget with benefits, costs and risks, instead of approving tools.
What does an IT strategy include?
A complete IT strategy has five pieces:
IT assessment: which systems support the operation today, how they integrate, which contracts and technical debt exist, and where current technology holds the business back.
Target architecture: how systems, data and infrastructure should be connected to execute the strategy, and what changes from the current state.
Prioritized portfolio of initiatives: the list of projects ordered by business impact, with their dependencies (an analytics project depends on the ERP's data, for example) and their sequence.
Business case per initiative: expected benefit, multi-year total cost — licenses, implementation, integrations, internal team, support — risk and owner.
IT governance: who decides on the portfolio, in which committee, with which indicators it is reviewed and how often it is updated.
An IT strategy without a business case per initiative is a list of projects. Without governance, it's a document no one opens again.
What is IT governance, and what do ISO/IEC 38500 and COBIT say?
IT governance is the part of the strategy that defines who decides and how the use of technology in the organization is controlled. Two public frameworks serve as references.

ISO/IEC 38500:2024, Information technology — Governance of IT for the organization, published in February 2024 in its third edition, provides guiding principles for members of governing bodies of organizations, and those who support them, on the effective, efficient and acceptable use of information technology. According to its official abstract, it applies to the governance of the organization's current and future use of IT and to organizations of all sizes — public and private companies, government entities and not-for-profits — regardless of the extent of their use of IT.

COBIT, published by ISACA, is described by its publisher as the premier framework for the governance and management of enterprise IT; its current version is COBIT 2019. Among what ISACA highlights is aligning IT goals with strategic business objectives, and the relationship between governance and management objectives, alignment goals and enterprise goals.

In our view, neither is adopted in full by a midsize company. ISO/IEC 38500 helps leadership understand its role — evaluating, directing and monitoring the use of technology; COBIT helps the IT team structure processes and controls. The IT strategy takes from each what the company's size and requirements justify.
How do you build an IT strategy, step by step?
1. Start from the business strategy. If it doesn't exist or isn't written down, the first step is strategic planning, not technology.
2. Assess what exists: systems, integrations, contracts, data and people. What works, what holds back and what it costs to maintain.
3. Define the target architecture: how systems, data and infrastructure should be connected to execute the strategy.
4. Identify and prioritize initiatives with a single criterion: business impact, dependencies, risk and the organization's capacity to absorb change.
5. Build the business case for the heaviest initiatives, with multi-year total cost and an owner.
6. Define governance: committee, indicators, review frequency and the criteria any vendor will be evaluated against later.
7. Execute and review: the strategy is adjusted when the business changes, not when the calendar says so.
Mistakes to avoid in an IT strategy

In our view, the costliest are four. Choosing the software before defining the architecture, so the tool ends up dictating the process. Planning without an owner per initiative, so the project gets whatever time is left over. Calculating only the license and not the multi-year total cost. And not reviewing the portfolio when the business changes, so the strategy becomes a historical document.
When does IT strategy consulting make sense?

When the company will invest in several systems over the coming years and has no map of what comes first; when departments buy tools on their own and nothing integrates; when the board asks for a technology plan with costs and benefits before approving a budget; or when the company needs senior technology leadership but doesn't have the daily decision volume to justify a full-time CIO or CTO.
How we can help

At Cyrrus we provide IT strategy consulting as part of the Construct phase of the CIRA method: assessment, target architecture, a prioritized portfolio with the business case for each initiative, and the criteria we later use to select software and infrastructure with no vendor bias. The same team that does the assessment accompanies execution.

If what's missing is the business strategy, we start with strategy consulting and strategic planning. And if the company needs technology leadership without a full-time position, we offer CIO and CTO as a Service.

body.text: What cybersecurity consulting includes

A security maturity assessment is not a vulnerability scan. A scan checks for known exposures in your systems. An assessment is more comprehensive: it inventories assets, reviews controls, interviews stakeholders, maps threats to business impact and produces a scored, prioritized remediation roadmap with an executive summary and a risk heat map. Its output is actionable; a raw scan list usually is not.

Beyond assessments, the services of cybersecurity consultants typically cover several areas. Security architecture includes zero-trust design, identity and access management (IAM), cloud landing zones and network segmentation. Governance, risk and compliance (GRC) work maps controls to frameworks and standards such as NIST CSF, ISO/IEC 27001, SOC 2 and PCI DSS. Incident response consulting covers readiness planning, playbooks, tabletop exercises and retainer-based response access. Penetration testing and red-team exercises are often scoped separately, so read the statement of work carefully before assuming they are included.

Those frameworks are not interchangeable. NIST CSF 2.0, published on February 26, 2024, organizes cybersecurity outcomes into six functions (govern, identify, protect, detect, respond and recover) and does not prescribe how to achieve them. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 defines the requirements of an information security management system and allows certification. PCI DSS, according to the PCI Security Standards Council, is a baseline of technical and operational requirements to protect payment account data, aimed at entities that store, process or transmit cardholder data. And SOC 2 is one of the assurance report offerings that CPAs can issue on the controls of a service organization, according to the AICPA, with criteria it names as security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality and privacy.

Many engagements also include evaluating security tools and third-party vendors, not just reviewing your current posture. The best firms do this using criteria defined by your business, without receiving commissions from the vendors they evaluate. That distinction is easy to miss when comparing proposals, and it matters a great deal in practice.
What signals tell you it is time to call a consultant

CEOs and CFOs notice the business-level signals: a near-miss breach, a contract requirement for SOC 2 or ISO/IEC 27001 that the internal team cannot meet, a cyber insurance renewal with new technical conditions, or board pressure after a competitor’s public incident. CFOs also feel the approval tension of signing security budgets without a return framework or a measurable outcome map.

CIOs and CTOs feel the structural friction: a tool stack that grew through reactive purchases with no unifying architecture, a vendor-recommended platform that underdelivered, or a cloud migration planned with no security layer. There is also the integrator conflict: the firm that sold you the platform also implements it and assesses it. That is not a staffing problem, it is an incentive problem.

The mistake that makes every signal worse is waiting. As an illustration, a company that discovers its vendor managed access with no audit trail only when a large customer reviews its suppliers could have caught that gap much earlier with a proactive assessment. A late discovery like that rarely comes cheaply, in time or in money.
Why vendor neutrality changes the outcome

Integrators who earn commissions from vendors have an incentive to recommend what they know and what pays, not necessarily what fits. The result can be overpayment, underperformance and a dependency that is hard to exit. This is not a judgment of character: it is a structural incentive.

The alternative is a consultancy that evaluates vendors against criteria your business defines, earns no commission from any platform and stays accountable from strategy through go-live. When one party owns both the advice and the outcome, the incentives finally align with yours. Cyrrus Consulting Services operates on this model: it evaluates providers against criteria defined by the business and with no commissions, and its external PMO function governs execution through go-live as the client’s advocate against the technology vendor. One team, one accountable party.
How a structured path moves you from diagnosis to adoption

A modern security maturity assessment looks different when AI is integrated into the diagnostic from the start: data collection speeds up and pattern recognition across controls is faster. Cyrrus Intelligence Lab designs AI governance, architecture and automation to support diagnosis and adoption.

Objective technology selection follows: defined evaluation criteria, structured scoring and an independent recommendation. The Cyrrus PMO then governs execution through go-live, protecting the client’s interests against vendor timeline drift and scope creep. The methodology moves through four phases (Construct, Identify, Realize and Adopt), connecting strategy to operation under a single accountable team.

Where cybersecurity engagements fail most is not at delivery but at sustainment. Cyrrus Leadership Academy addresses this directly: it trains the client’s own team to operate and iterate on the security model independently after the project closes. For a CFO, that is the difference between a measurable outcome and a report that collects dust.
How much to budget and which engagement model fits

As a public reference, Clutch (page updated September 21, 2026) reports that the average cost of hiring a cybersecurity provider on its platform is US$100–149 per hour, with location averages of US$150–199 in the United States and US$50–99 in Mexico, Spain and Poland. Cybersecurity projects reviewed on Clutch typically cost US$10,000–49,999. Clutch does not publish the sample size behind these figures, so use them to orient yourself, not to quote. In our view, the variables that move the price most are the number of sites and applications, the depth of testing, regulatory requirements and whether the work is advisory only or includes implementation.

How to shortlist a firm and which questions filter out the wrong ones

For governance and compliance work, in our view you should verify certifications such as CISM, which ISACA presents as the credential that affirms the ability to assess risks, implement effective governance and proactively respond to incidents, along with equivalents such as CISSP and CISA for program and audit roles. For penetration testing, look for credentials in that specialty, and for ISO/IEC 27001 engagements, the lead auditor credential. What matters is that every credential you verify belongs to the people assigned to your engagement, not to someone elsewhere in the firm.

A strong case study includes a client of comparable industry and size, a specific measurable outcome and evidence that improvements persisted after delivery. A redacted sample report should prioritize findings by business impact, with named owners and remediation guidance. A generic control checklist is not a deliverable.
These seven questions expose weak claims before you sign:
1. Which named consultants will perform the work, and what are their individual credentials? A strong answer names people; a weak answer names the firm.
2. What percentage of delivery will be done by senior practitioners? Follow up if the answer is vague or the percentage seems low.
3. Is the firm an advisor, an authorized assessor, or both? Some frameworks require independence between the two roles; know which applies to your situation.
4. Does the firm receive any compensation from the vendors it recommends? The answer should be a clear and unambiguous no.

5. Can they provide a redacted sample deliverable and a comparable client reference? Refusing to show any deliverable is a reasonable warning sign unless confidentiality constraints are explained and mitigated.
6. How are findings tracked, retested and reported to executives between engagements? Findings should not appear only in an annual summary report.
7. How is evidence maintained between audits rather than collected only before one? This separates firms that build programs from firms that build reports.

body.text: The scene repeats in many boardrooms: sales presents one revenue figure, finance another, and the next twenty minutes go to arguing which one is true instead of what to do about it. The problem isn't the dashboard or the system: no one decided which source the official figure comes from or who answers for it.

This guide explains what data governance is, what the international standard says about the role of governing bodies, how it differs from data quality and data management, what leadership must decide and how to start without a year-long project.
What is data governance?

Data governance is the set of decisions and rules that define who owns each data set, which system its official version comes from, which quality rules apply when it is captured and transformed, who may use it and for what. It is not a tool or a cleanup project: it is the decision structure that keeps the cleanup from having to be repeated every year.

ISO/IEC 38505-1:2026, Information technology — Governance of data — Part 1, published in August 2026 in its second edition, defines the governance of data as a subset or domain of the governance of IT, which is itself a subset of organizational or corporate governance. In other words: governing data is a responsibility of the company's governance, not only of the IT department.
What does ISO/IEC 38505-1 say about the role of leadership?

According to its official abstract, the standard provides principles for governing bodies of organizations — owners, directors, partners, executive managers or similar — on the effective, efficient and acceptable use of data, by applying the governance principles and model of ISO/IEC 38500 to the governance of data, assuring stakeholders and informing and guiding governing bodies in the use and protection of data.

It applies to the governance of the current and future use of data created, collected, stored, secured, protected or controlled by IT systems, and to organizations of all sizes regardless of how much they depend on data. It also guides executive managers, external specialists, service providers (including consultants) and auditors.
If the standard addresses data governance to owners and directors, the question for leadership isn't which tool to buy, but which decisions are theirs.
What is the difference between data governance, data management and data quality?

Three things that get mixed up are worth separating. Data governance decides: owners, official version, rules and who may use what. Data management executes: it captures, integrates, stores, protects and delivers data according to those rules; the DAMA-DMBOK, published by DAMA International, is the recognized reference framework for that management. Data quality is an outcome: completeness, uniqueness, validity and consistency of the data that management produces under the rules governance defined.

When a company 'cleans the CRM' every year and the duplicates come back, what's missing isn't more cleaning: it's governance. No one decided who owns the customer record or which rule prevents creating a customer that already exists.
What must leadership decide?
Five decisions, in our view, cannot be delegated to the IT department:
Domains and owners: which data domains exist (customers, products, suppliers, finance, people) and who answers for each, by name.
Official version: which system the figure the board sees comes from — sales from the CRM or the ERP, inventory from the ERP or the WMS — and why.
Minimum rules: which fields are mandatory, what prevents duplicates, who validates a change to master data.
Access and use: who may view, change and export each domain, and which data stays out of reach of any artificial intelligence model.
Review: how often the catalog is reviewed, who measures quality and whom it is reported to.
How do you start with data governance, step by step?

1. Choose two or three critical domains, not all of them. Customers and products are usually the starting point in our projects, because they live in the CRM and the ERP and feed sales, invoicing and inventory.
2. Run a short assessment: which systems generate that data, where it is duplicated (spreadsheets included) and which figures don't reconcile between departments.
3. Name an owner per domain and define the official version. It's the decision that prevents the most arguments later.
4. Write the minimum capture, deduplication and access rules, and enforce them in the systems that already exist: mandatory fields, validations and duplicate detection in the CRM and the ERP.
5. Build the catalog of critical data and its lineage: where every indicator the board sees comes from.
6. Define the controls for AI: which data a model may use, which it may not, and with what traceability. This is the bridge to AI governance.
7. Measure and review: duplicates, empty fields, figures that reconcile. Without measurement, rules loosen within months.
Do you need a data governance tool?

Not at first. Capture, deduplication and access rules are enforced first in the CRM and ERP that already exist. A catalog or data quality tool is evaluated later, once owners and rules are defined, and with the same vendor-independent criteria used in any software selection. Buying the tool before naming the owners is, in our view, the fastest way to get a catalog nobody maintains.
How does it relate to AI governance?

Data governance is the foundation of AI governance. A model is only auditable if it is known which data it used, where it came from and who answered for its quality; and it is only safe if it is written down which data it may not touch. That is why data controls for AI are defined within data governance and integrated into the AI governance framework, not as a separate project.

body.text: Three artificial intelligence proposals reach the committee: a customer service assistant, a demand forecasting model and a tool that 'automates everything' in the back office. Each comes with a flawless demo. What doesn't come is the criterion to decide which is worth it, in what order and what it takes to make it work with the data and systems the company actually has.

This guide explains what an AI strategy is, how it differs from buying tools, how use cases are prioritized, what NIST's public framework says about managing risk from design, how the roadmap is built and which decisions belong to leadership.
What is an AI strategy?

An AI strategy answers three questions: in which business processes artificial intelligence changes a measurable outcome, in what order it's worth doing, and what it takes — data, systems, governance, people — for it to work in production and not only in a demonstration. Its output is a roadmap: a short list of prioritized use cases with sequence, owners, dependencies and how each will be measured.
It is not a list of tools or a statement of intent. It is an investment decision, with the same rigor as any other initiative in the company's technology portfolio.
What is the difference between an AI strategy and buying AI tools?

The order. Buying tools starts from what a vendor offers and looks afterwards for where to apply it; a strategy starts from the processes and data that already exist and decides afterwards which technology, if any, improves them. The first route produces what we see in our projects: five tools bought by five departments that don't talk to each other, and pilots that never reach production because the data they needed never existed.
The question isn't what AI can do. It's which process in your company changes an outcome if done differently, and what it takes to do it differently.
How do you prioritize AI use cases?
With a single criterion applied to every candidate, so the committee compares like with like. In our view, four dimensions are enough:
Impact: which business outcome changes — cycle time, errors, cost, revenue — and how much that change is worth.
Feasibility: whether the necessary technology exists and is proven, and whether the team can operate it.
Data: whether the data the case needs exists, with what quality, who owns it and whether it may be used for that purpose.
Risk: what happens if the model is wrong, who is affected and which controls are needed.
The result is a short, ordered list with what each case needs before it starts. What has no data or owner isn't discarded: it is postponed until data governance resolves it.
What does the NIST AI RMF say about managing AI risk?

The AI Risk Management Framework from the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology is a framework intended for voluntary use to incorporate trustworthiness into the design, development, use and evaluation of AI systems. Version 1.0 was released on January 26, 2023, and NIST notes it is being revised. Its core organizes risk management into four functions: Govern, Map, Measure and Manage.

In July 2024 NIST published the Generative AI Profile (NIST-AI-600-1), which helps identify the risks specific to that technology. For an AI strategy, the framework's practical value is that it forces you to define, case by case and before building, which risk is accepted, who answers and how it will be measured; which framework the company adopts to govern AI is a leadership decision we cover in the AI governance guide.
How do you build the AI roadmap, step by step?

1. Inventory the AI already in use: which tools exist, who bought them, which data they work with and what result they give. In many companies the strategy starts by putting in order what already exists.
2. Discover use cases with the departments, not with the vendor: processes with volume, repetitiveness, available data and a known current cost.
3. Prioritize with the single criterion (impact, feasibility, data, risk) and produce a short list.
4. Define for each case how it will be measured: the real process before and after — time, errors, cost, revenue — never the demo.
5. Resolve the dependencies: data (governance and quality), integrations (architecture) and controls (AI governance). A case with unresolved dependencies doesn't enter the roadmap.
6. Sequence and assign owners: what comes first, what depends on what, who answers for each case in the business, not in IT.
7. Execute the first cases as measured pilots, and review the roadmap with the real results.
What must leadership decide?

Approve the prioritized list with the same criterion for every case. Decide which data no model may touch and who answers for each use case. Choose the AI governance framework. And review the measurement: if a case didn't change the real process, it stops, even if the demo is still flawless.
