body.text: The question most executives ask is which firm has the best AI credentials. The better question is a different one: who accepts accountability for the result, not just the deliverable?
What end-to-end AI consulting should cover

In our view, a serious AI strategy engagement begins with use-case discovery, ROI modeling and a readiness assessment covering data, infrastructure, talent and processes. The output should be a prioritized roadmap tied to business outcomes, not a list of ideas. A strategy with no execution owner attached is not a complete service.

The full implementation lifecycle runs from discovery through a validated pilot, production architecture, integration, controlled launch, stabilization and continuous improvement. Each phase leaves concrete deliverables: a working prototype, benchmark results, runbooks and monitoring dashboards. A firm that exits after the pilot report leaves the client’s team alone with the production risk.

That is the gap Cyrrus’s CIRA method is built to close. Its four phases (Construct, Identify, Realize and Adopt) connect strategy to operation under a single accountable team, with AI integrated to speed up diagnosis, vendor selection and execution. The same group that builds the roadmap stays accountable through go-live and adoption, with no handoff between strategy and implementation.
Why so many AI initiatives never reach production

The State of Enterprise AI 2026 report, by the software company Prosigns, is based on a survey of 1,200 leaders at companies with at least 500 employees and US$100 million in revenue, run between December 2025 and February 2026. According to that report, 82% of AI initiatives launched in 2024 had still not reached production by the first quarter of 2026, up from 73% in its 2024 baseline. Two caveats: it is a vendor’s report, and its sample over-represents companies that already have an AI system in production (38% of the sample, against the 15–18% the report itself estimates for the market), so treat it as a signal rather than a census.

The same report names data quality and availability as the main blocker to reaching production since it began tracking the question in 2022. What changed in 2026 is that governance and compliance review delays rose to second place: 31% of respondents cite them as a top blocker, up from 18% in 2024. It also mentions the lack of MLOps infrastructure (27%) and the senior talent gap (24%).

From there, in our view three failures are ones a serious firm should prevent from the contract onward. The first is biased recommendation: some firms are paid by the vendors they recommend, and that conflict undermines objectivity. The second is leaving change management for the end: without an adoption plan, the team does not use what was built. The third is missing governance: with no defined owners, monitoring or human oversight, an AI system in production is a liability with a user interface. Prosigns’ data does not measure adoption separately, so the second failure is a conclusion from our experience, not a figure.
Three requirements that are not negotiable

Vendor neutrality. Ask in writing whether the firm receives any compensation from the vendors it recommends, and have it confirmed before you proceed. Cyrrus evaluates platforms against criteria the business defines, with no commissions from recommended vendors.

Execution with an accountable owner through go-live. A roadmap with no execution owner shifts all implementation risk to your internal team. Ask who is responsible for monitoring and retraining the system after launch: it is one of the questions recommended by Futureproofing’s guide to AI vendor selection.

Structured adoption. Change management must be in scope from day one, with a training plan and a usage indicator. Its warning signs are low utilization, workarounds that users invent to avoid the system, and an executive team that cannot explain what return was delivered.
What it costs: reference ranges

Engagement models vary. Fixed price works when scope and acceptance criteria are clear; hourly billing fits exploratory work or changing requirements. Tillerbridge, a firm that sells fixed scope and therefore has its own interest, calls hourly billing the weakest of the three models for the buyer, because the meter rewards more hours and two hourly bids cannot be compared.
As a budgeting reference, Tillerbridge publishes the following 2026 ranges (the page was last reviewed in July 2026 and cites “published rate guides” without naming them):
Reference ranges for AI consulting (Tillerbridge, 2026)

Ask each candidate for a rate card, a not-to-exceed ceiling or example past proposals as evidence of pricing discipline. Check what proposals routinely leave out: cloud and model consumption costs, software licenses, internal staff time, data remediation, security review and legal work. A firm that quotes only its fees and leaves model consumption and integration labor unquantified is setting you up for a scope dispute months later.
How to vet a consulting firm before you sign

Ask for production references from organizations of comparable size and complexity. Case studies on a firm’s website are marketing material. Ask each reference whether the work reached production or stopped at proof of concept, what broke after launch and who fixed it. Also ask for an architecture and data-flow diagram for one of your use cases and an evaluation framework with task-specific tests, accuracy thresholds and a regression test plan. If the firm cannot produce those artifacts during selection, in our view that is a red flag.

In the contract, require: that the client owns the deliverables and the trained models; a ban on using your data to train models for others; return or deletion of data and handover of models, code and documentation on termination; and the current status (not a roadmap) of certifications such as ISO/IEC 27001 or SOC 2 Type II. For AI-specific security, ask for a threat model that covers at least the risks OWASP lists in its 2025 Top 10 for LLM Applications, including prompt injection (LLM01) and data and model poisoning (LLM04).

Five questions, in our view, separate strong firms from weak ones: Who owns the production system after go-live? What happens to your data if you terminate the engagement? Can the firm show results from a comparable deployment? Does it receive any compensation from the vendors it recommends? What does its change management program look like in practice? A capable partner answers all five directly.
From pilot to production: gates and ROI

Before authorizing any phase transition, in our view you should require: a named process owner, a baseline-measured indicator, accuracy and latency thresholds tested on production-like data, security review and access controls confirmed, monitoring dashboards and rollback capability live, and representative users trained. Skipping these gates is a frequent reason pilots stall in perpetual iteration without reaching production. Futureproofing’s guide also recommends that a paid pilot run on a representative slice of your data and test production readiness, including who owns monitoring and retraining.

ROI is not measured at the end: it is defined at the start, with a named indicator and a baseline measured before the pilot. So the client’s team can sustain operations and continuous improvement without depending on the consultancy, Cyrrus Leadership Academy builds internal capability inside the organization.
You do not choose an AI consulting firm for its credentials, but for who accepts accountability for the result.
How we can help

Cyrrus Consulting Services is built around this model: vendor-neutral recommendations, execution governed by an external PMO through go-live, and structured adoption. The CIRA method, Cyrrus Intelligence Lab and Leadership Academy exist because strategy and execution need to live under the same roof, with one team accountable from the first diagnostic to the last training session. body.text: The ERP contract is signed, the integrator has a work plan and the vendor has a schedule. One question remains that no vendor document answers: who, on the company's side, is accountable for the project delivering what the committee approved in scope, time and cost.

This guide explains what a PMO does in an ERP implementation, which areas project governance must cover according to a vendor's public guide, who decides what, what tends to be cut first when the budget tightens, how the PMO's work is measured and what leadership must decide before signing.
What does a PMO do in an ERP implementation?

It governs the project. Microsoft's Dynamics 365 implementation guide defines project governance as the framework and techniques that help you map business goals to actions and measures, structure and plan the project, anticipate and avoid issues, detect and correct risks, and respond to change. In practice, that is the job of an external PMO on an ERP project.

The same guide stresses something worth bringing to the committee: an ERP project is not only a technical project, it is a business transformation project that affects, and is affected by, the processes and the people in the business. That is why governance must involve the business and not stay inside the IT team.

In our view, the practical difference is this: the integrator is accountable for delivering and configuring the system; the PMO is accountable to leadership for the project as a whole moving toward the approved goals, with a single place where risks, scope changes and pending decisions are recorded.
Which areas must ERP project governance cover?

Microsoft's guide lists six areas of governance that, according to the document itself, are relevant to any implementation methodology. Although it is written for Microsoft products, it works as a public checklist to review any ERP project:
Project goals: clear, measurable goals that give direction and focus, aligned with business objectives.
Project organization: the structure and roles that make the project efficient and effective.
Project approach: the methodology that fits the scope, complexity and constraints.
Classic structures: change, risk and issue management, and how effective they are.
Key project areas: solution design, testing and deployment, which the guide says often get technical attention but lack sufficient direction, planning and oversight.
Project plan: a well-structured plan that lets you track and improve progress and outcomes.

The guide recommends defining the governance model as early as possible, preferably in the initiate phase, because it determines the approach, oversight, resources and plan, and reviewing it throughout the project.
Who decides what: steering committee and implementation team?

Microsoft groups roles into two structures. The steering committee is a group of senior stakeholders with the authority to keep the project team aligned with the KPIs: as they monitor progress, they can make decisions that affect the overall strategy, including budget, costs and expected functionality. It usually consists of senior management and the leaders of the business groups included in the rollout.

The core implementation team does the actual execution. According to the guide, it includes project managers, business subject matter experts, solution architects, functional and technical consultants, developers, testers, trainers, adoption and change management advisors and user champions. The guide warns that the lack of availability of any of these roles may cause delays, an incomplete understanding of the processes and poor user adoption.

When there is an outside integrator, the guide asks that the statement of work (SoW) not stop at high-level activities: it should detail activities, assumptions, roles and responsibilities, and what is out of scope. It describes the risk this way: the customer assumes the integrator will handle an activity while the integrator assumes the customer will. The activities it lists include process modeling, data migration, integration with other systems, test strategy and execution, orchestration of user acceptance tests, security and role design, cutover planning and execution, and adoption and change management.
What gets cut first when the budget tightens?

Microsoft's implementation strategy guide says it plainly: as scope and timelines change, activities toward the end of the lifecycle are often cut to meet budget constraints, and it names performance testing, data validation testing, training and change management. It adds that this can significantly affect the quality and success of the implementation.

That is a concrete reason to have a PMO: someone with a mandate from the committee to defend those activities when the schedule tightens, or to document what was decided to cut and who approved it. body.text: How is the PMO's work measured?

Microsoft's guide asks you to agree, from the start, on concrete indicators of project success and use them to prioritize scope. It also asks for constant assessment of the variance between budget and actual cost throughout the project lifecycle.
Based on that, in our view leadership can ask the PMO for a short, stable dashboard with these items:
Milestones met against the approved plan, and deviations with their cause.
Variance between budget and actual cost, with the projection at completion.
Open risks, each with an owner, a date and an action.
Requested, decided scope changes and their effect on timeline and cost.
Availability of the process owners and user champions the plan assumed.
Status of the closing activities that tend to be cut: testing, data validation, training and change management.
What must leadership decide before signing?

Who chairs project governance and who sits on the steering committee. That the contract with the integrator details activities, assumptions and roles. What budget and timeline are protected for the end-of-project activities. Which indicators will measure success. And which methodology fits the company's culture: Microsoft's guide notes that organizations used to a traditional approach, such as waterfall, may need more change management planning to adopt an agile or hybrid one.

If you have not chosen the ERP yet, settle that decision first: the guide to the best ERP for mid-sized companies sorts the options, and the total cost calculator helps estimate the budget over several years.
